lines.text: For 600 years, a monastery in the Carpathian mountains rang its bell every hour. Day and night.
Not once did it miss an hour. Not in plague. Not in war.
The monks never said why. The villagers below never asked.
Last winter, the last monk died.
At 3 a.m., the bell went silent for the first time in six centuries.
In the valley, every dog turned toward the mountain and howled.
But the strangest part wasn't the silence.
It was the fog. It came down from the peaks and stopped above the monastery.
At sunrise, the villagers saw a shape in it.
A brow. A nose. Two closed eyelids. Larger than the mountain.
Every hour the bell didn't ring, the eyelids opened a little more.
A shepherd climbed up to ring it. The rope had been cut. From above.
Inside, the monks had kept a log. One line for every hour, for 600 years.
Every line said the same word. Asleep.
The oldest page wasn't written in any language the monks knew.
Then historians looked at other bells.
Medieval bells carried an inscription: I call the living. I mourn the dead. I break the lightning.
On some bells, a fourth line had been scratched out.
In the Second World War, Nazi Germany took 175,000 bells from Europe's towers and melted them.
That winter, villages under the empty towers reported the same fog.
On the seventh night, the villagers carried their own church bell up the mountain.
They hung it with their hands bleeding.
Above them, the eyes were already open.
It was looking at the village.
Then the bell rang. And the eyes slowly closed.
Not all the way.
The road to the monastery was closed. A new monk was sent. No one knows where they found him.
Somewhere near you, a bell still rings every hour. Nobody remembers why.
Maybe the question isn't why they ring. Maybe it's who will ring them when we're gone.
